chapter: Return to Chicago: the Blue Note and Rupneck's
title: George Brunis at the microphone and Wild Bill's salary
summary: The band drinks, Brunis hogs the mike while Sarah Vaughan waits, and he refuses to let Wild Bill earn more. The Blue Note job ends after 11 weeks.

story.theme_name: Band pranks, jokes and gigs gone wrong

blocks.x: brother in law's house, I saw that he ate, I took him with his drums to the Blue Note, I set him up. I was a Zottie fan. And within days, he's not talking to me. And he's mad at me, which is worse, and he's evil.

Now that's going on. Now they start to drinking. I've got George Brunis, one Saturday night, five bottles are consumed, either three pints or three fifths, or two pints -- whatever it is, between who? Pee Wee, Zotty, George Brunis, maybe Chippy had a sip or something. She wasn't great on drinking. So this was going on. And Frank Holstein -- now, George Brunis is getting up in front of the mike, and Frank says to me, whatever you do, I don't care what else you do, beat him to the mike. To try to beat George Brunis, and Sarah Vaughan is waiting to go on.
And George grabs the mike away from him. And says, 'my mother thinks I'm selling stolen cars in Pittsburgh, but I'm not as you can see. I want to tell you about a tune I wrote.'
MR. DEMICHAEL: he wrote my records... in City Hall.

MR. HODES: And Frank Holstein is turning off the mike. Now, Frank Holstein is standing on the -- where you can't -- the audience can't see you, but he's at the bandstand behind the curtain, like, where the band can see him. And he's kneeling down and he's calling with his little finger to Brunis to get away from the piano and Brunis isn't getting away. He's doing ten, 15 minutes.

Now, this is the scene. We got everything facing us. Now the next deal, let's get Wild Bill. I call Wild Bill, he wants $275. I says to Brunis, in our meeting with the band, let's give it to him. I'll keep track of the books, you won't lose a dime. When we hit the road and start making money, he still gets $275 and we get more, and we build it up that we all get even.
'That son of a bitch ain't going to get a dime more than me, he ain't worth it.'
So, of course, there went that idea. And then the dickering -- and Fred Williamson discovered that I couldn't handle those guys, which was true.

That's it. I found that nobody could handle them. They just were not going to be handled. And he must have had an idea about me, based on what happened in New York. But at that time, Brunis was not the Brunis that I met in Chicago. When I played (unintelligible) with Brunis, George was not that same George. In those next years, he had changed more or something.
